transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-27 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Lina Zhou (Redwood Product), Carlos Mendez (Reefmark Head of ML), Priya Raman (Reefmark Platform), Dave Liu (CTO), Sara Bloom (Procurement)

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everybody, thanks for joining. quick roll call?
[00:06] Carlos Mendez: carlos here.
[00:08] Priya Raman: priya here.
[00:09] Dave Liu: dave here.
[00:11] Sara Bloom: sara here.
[00:13] Ethan Cole: ethan, good to meet you all.
[00:15] Maya Patel: cool. objective — want to understand your cost constraints, performance targets, and who needs to sign off for pilot. we'll talk through hosted/dedicated/private tradeoffs, batching and cache levers, and propose a pilot. ok?

[00:28] Carlos: yup. to set context, reefmark is building a routing recommendation engine for last-mile deliveries. real-time scoring on incoming events, typical seq lengths around 350 tokens, occasionally up to 1k. target p99 latency under 200ms for the critical path, but we'd accept 300ms if cost savings are significant. budget is tight — we have an initial pilot budget of about $12k/month, and if numbers line up we'll expand.

[01:02] Ethan: thanks, that's helpful. rough question up front — are you more focused on minimizing per-token cost or on deterministic latency and isolation? because that steers toward hosted vs dedicated vs private.

[01:12] Dave: both, honestly. for production we need isolation (can't send route data to multi-tenant without controls) but for the pilot we could try hosted if you can guarantee data residency and less exposure. our security team flagged SOC2, SSO (SAML), and KMS integration as gating factors.

[01:29] Lina Zhou: we can do SSO, and our hosted API supports customer-managed keys for encryption at rest via K M S integrations; for full HSM-backed keys we have private deployment options as well.

[01:40] Priya: great — can you explain first-order unit economics? like per-token cost on hosted vs dedicated with batching and cache?

[01:47] Maya: sure. I'll give an example to anchor the math. imagine your model usage is 1M tokens per day — that's ~30M tokens/month. on hosted we price per token (input+output) — for this example let's use a ballpark that isn't a quote but to illustrate tradeoffs. with some workload-aware batching and a 1-2x KV prefix cache hit rate you might see effective per-token cost drop by 35-50% vs naive per-request runs.

[02:20] Carlos: can you show the math quickly?

[02:23] Maya: yeah. if raw hosted list price is X per token, after batching and cache you effectively amortize GPU compute over more tokens. for example, with 4x batching and 25% prefix cache hits, the marginal cost per token can look like 0.6X. on dedicated, you move to reserved capacity — so cost becomes more of a fixed monthly commitment (GPU pool) plus lower per-token run cost for sustained throughput. rough breakeven for dedicated vs hosted in our experience is when you exceed consistent daily volume of around 800k–1.2M tokens depending on model/seq-length.

[03:02] Priya: when you say 4x batching, what's the latency impact? our p99 requirements are strict.

[03:08] Ethan: good question. batching is a latency vs throughput trade. with continuous batching and dynamic SLOs our runtime tries to keep p99 within target by only batching up to a configured latency budget. for example, you can set a 30ms batching window — most requests will go out immediately, some will wait up to 30ms to be batched. that can increase p50 a little but p99 is kept under control if you calibrate properly. we also do automatic fallbacks to lower-cost variants if queues build up.

[03:44] Dave: hmm. that 30ms adds up. our current real-time path budgets 100ms for network + compute; adding batching delays might push over 200ms. are there other levers?

[03:55] Maya: yes — KV caching can be huge for repeated prefixes (your prompts often share similar headers). if prefix hit rate is high, you avoid re-computing initial layers and you see big latency and cost wins. plus, quantized model variants on dedicated or private can reduce per-token compute while maintaining acceptable quality.

[04:15] Carlos: we do have a lot of repeated system prompts and many short completions. maybe cache will help. what about burst capacity? on delivery spikes we need throughput for peak hours.

[04:25] Ethan: dedicated includes configurable burst capacity and autoscaling policies. you reserve baseline GPUs for predictable throughput and configure burst pools that spin up when you hit thresholds. for Private (VPC/on-prem) you control the infra fully; burst is up to you and your cloud infra design. hosted has soft limits but we can negotiate higher reserved throughput for pilots.

[04:48] Priya: what's the unit-econ comparison for a short completion workload vs long seqs? we have mix — most are short (<100 tokens) but some longer ones.

[04:57] Maya: short completions are more sensitive to per-request overhead (KV cache helps), long seqs consume more tokens per inference and are impacted by throughput and memory constraints (KV cache also reduces effective tokens if prefix repeats). overall, the per-token price can be lower for long streaming outputs because of amortized attention compute, but latency per request increases. we'll put together an example calc using your sequence distribution.

[05:23] Dave: security again — for private we need proof of controls, audit logs, and ability to use our KMS. is that all supported?

[05:31] Lina: yes. Private supports customer VPC, peering, and HSM/KMS integration. we provide audit logs and per-token tracing hooks in the console. we also have SOC2 reports we can share. hosted can optionally be configured with customer-managed keys for at-rest encryption; dedicated gives stronger isolation with dedicated GPU pools.

[05:51] Sara: procurement needs rough pricing to budget. we can't sign open-ended high per-token costs. how flexible are pilots? can we cap spend?

[05:59] Maya: pilots are commonly structured with a fixed monthly cap and defined usage lanes. we can set hard token caps and alerts; if you hit them we'll throttle or route to a lower-cost model variant. we can also do a reserved pilot (committed capacity) which lowers unit pricing.

[06:18] Carlos: I'd like to see a scenario: 30M tokens/month, mix 80% short (<=100), 20% long (~350), target p99 <=200ms, and cap $12k/month. can you show feasibility?

[06:31] Ethan: quick back-of-envelope — we'll take that offline and return a calc but qualitatively: if cache hits are 20–30% and batching average ~3x for the short path, hosted could be close but might exceed the cap. dedicated reserved could push unit costs down but requires commit; private is likely too heavy for pilot unless you already have infra. we'll run cost modelling with your sample traces.

[06:54] Priya: okay. what about model choices — you host open models or do you recommend Redwood-verified variants?

[07:01] Lina: we have a catalog of curated open models with performance profiles. for production we often recommend quantized variants or smaller distilled models for routing tasks — they hit latency targets and are cheaper. we can A/B test quality on your prompts in the benchmark.

[07:18] Dave: any network considerations for VPC peering? we operate in AWS us-east-1.

[07:24] Ethan: Private supports AWS, GCP, Azure patterns; VPC peering or private link are standard. we'll share the network diagram checklist. latency over peering is usually single-digit ms in-region.

[07:36] Carlos: what's the SLA for Dedicated? we need availability guarantees if this goes to prod routing.

[07:41] Maya: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in our enterprise tiers. we'll share the SLA doc. Pilot typically runs without full enterprise SLA but we can negotiate for reserved pilots.

[07:55] Sara: procurement question: do you require a minimum term for dedicated?

[07:59] Maya: yes, dedicated is usually committed monthly or annually depending on discount tier. pilot reserved capacity can be monthly. we'll propose options in pricing sheet.

[08:10] Carlos: ok, action items? we want the pricing + a concrete benchmark plan. also need SOC2 and security docs.

[08:17] Maya: noted — we'll send pricing, SOC2, private deployment checklist, and a benchmark plan. Ethan will run the benchmark with your sample traffic.

[08:25] Ethan: for the benchmark, we want a 24–72 hour trace and a few representative prompts per path. we'll run p50/p95/p99 latency and token burn comparisons across hosted, a dedicated reserved config, and a quantized variant.

[08:41] Priya: timeline — can we start the benchmark in the week of Oct 4?

[08:44] Maya: yes that's doable. we'll target to deliver pricing and docs by Oct 1, benchmark plan by Oct 2, and kickoff the benchmark Oct 5.

[08:52] Dave: decision maker note — if numbers fit, Dave + Carlos + Sara sign off; procurement will need PO.

[08:58] Sara: yep.

[09:00] Maya: recap: we'll send pilot pricing with hosted vs dedicated vs private rows, include examples with your seq distribution and a $12k cap scenario; share SOC2 and private deploy checklist; schedule benchmark week of Oct 4; draft SOW for 4–6 week pilot. any other questions?

[09:16] Carlos: one more — curious about multi-region fallback. if us-east has outage, can you fallback to another region without data egress issues?

[09:26] Lina: yes — routing policies can prefer region and fallback to another. for private deployments you'd control egress, but we can design cross-region fallbacks in Dedicated with encryption in transit and residency controls noted in the SOW.

[09:40] Priya: great. thanks everyone.
[09:42] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up by end of week.
[09:46] END
